newsitem.title: UK: Canadian mine development spending to soar in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Canadian mine development spending to soar in 1997.

text.p: Mineral exploration and mine development in Canada is booming again after a slump during the 1980s, officials at a seminar said.
"Development spending is racing up," Keith Brewer, an official with Natural Resources Canada, told a government-sponsored seminar in London.

Capital spending on new mines in Canada is forecast to more than triple to C$1.7 billion in 1997 from C$500 million this year, said Brewer, director general of mining and minerals financial analysis for the government agency.
Capital spending should plateau at around C$2.5 billion from 1998 to 2000, he added.
Exploration spending in Canada increased about C$200 million to C$900 million in 1996 and should remain steady this year, Brewer said.
As the Canadian mining sector has matured, large companies are relying more and more on junior firms to undertake exploration.

"It is becoming increasingly apparent that a number of major Canadian mining companies are withdrawing from the mineral exploration business as they have been unable to compete with the exploration success of the Canadian juniors," said Steve Vaughan, a Toronto lawyer and a director of the Prospectors and Developers Association of Canada.
"What we are seeing is the segmenting of the industry and allowing its various component parts to specialise in those areas of the mineral business in which they excel," he added.
About C$550 million of the C$900 million exploration spending was by small firms whose total exploration budgets were less than C$4 million, Brewer said.
The mining industry was in decline during the 1980s, suffering a dive of nearly 50 percent in capital investment between 1981 and 1991, said Vaughan.

But the Whitehorse Mining Initiative launched in 1992 brought together groups which have a stake in the mining industry, including companies, labour groups, environmental organisations, aboriginal groups, government and industry associations.
The groups were able to reach consensus on many issues and signed an accord in September 1994, said Vaughan, who participated in the initiative.
